mcqs.q: Simple extraction is also known as:
opts: Closed extraction, forceps technique, or intra-alveolar extraction
mcqs.explain: Surgical extraction is the open method, also called trans-alveolar extraction.

mcqs.q: How many major motions can the forceps apply?
mcqs.explain: Apical pressure, buccal force, lingual/palatal pressure, rotational pressure and tractional force.

mcqs.q: Apical pressure achieves expansion of the tooth socket by:
opts: Insertion of the beaks of the forceps down into the periodontal ligament space
Turning the tooth within its socket
Pulling the tooth in an occlusal direction
Rocking the tooth buccally and lingually
mcqs.explain: The beak acts as a wedge to expand the alveolar bone and displace the tooth occlusally.

mcqs.q: The beak of the forceps acts as a:
opts: Wedge, to expand the alveolar bone and displace the tooth occlusally
Lever, with the crestal bone as fulcrum
Clamp, to grip the crown of the tooth
mcqs.explain: This is the mechanical basis of apical pressure.

mcqs.q: Buccal pressure results in expansion of the:
opts: Buccal alveolar plate, particularly at the crest of the ridge, with lingual apical pressure
Lingual plate at the crest only
mcqs.explain: Lingual/palatal pressure is aimed at expanding the lingual bone.

mcqs.q: Rotational pressure is mostly used to luxate:
mcqs.explain: Slender or multi-rooted teeth are more likely to fracture under this type of force.

mcqs.q: Rotational forces are mainly limited to the conical roots of the:
opts: Upper central incisor and lower second premolar
Upper lateral incisor and lower first premolar
Upper first premolar and lower first molar
mcqs.explain: These are the two teeth named as suitable for rotation.

mcqs.q: Tractional force should be:
opts: Limited to the final portion of the extraction process and gentle
Applied from the very beginning of the extraction
mcqs.explain: It is useful for delivering the tooth only once adequate bony expansion is achieved.

mcqs.q: Maxillary teeth are usually removed by:
opts: Strong buccal forces and less vigorous palatal forces
Strong palatal forces and less vigorous buccal forces
mcqs.explain: The maxillary buccal bone is usually thinner than the palatal cortical bone.

mcqs.q: In the mandible, which teeth usually require a STRONGER lingual pressure?
mcqs.explain: The buccal bone is thinner from the midline posteriorly to the premolars, but the mandibular molars have stronger buccal bone.

mcqs.q: The major portion of the extraction force is always directed toward:
opts: The thinnest and therefore weakest bone
mcqs.explain: This single principle explains the technique for every tooth in both jaws.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of the five general steps of forceps extraction?
opts: Loosen soft tissue → luxate with elevator → adapt forceps → luxate with forceps → remove
Adapt forceps → loosen soft tissue → luxate with elevator → luxate with forceps → remove
Luxate with elevator → loosen soft tissue → adapt forceps → remove → luxate with forceps
Loosen soft tissue → adapt forceps → remove → luxate with elevator → luxate with forceps
mcqs.explain: The elevator step is used if indicated.

mcqs.q: The instrument used to loosen the soft tissue attachment is the:
opts: Sharp end of a periosteal elevator (No. 9 Molt)
mcqs.explain: It allows the forceps to be positioned more apically without interference from the soft tissue.

mcqs.q: Loosening and slightly reflecting the gingiva before extraction:
opts: Increases the width of the gingival sulcus and allows easy entrance of the forceps beaks
Prevents fracture of the alveolar bone
Removes the need for an elevator
mcqs.explain: It also lets the forceps be positioned more apically.

mcqs.q: In step II, the elevator of choice is the:
mcqs.explain: It is inserted perpendicular or parallel to the tooth into the interdental space after reflecting the interdental papilla.

mcqs.q: Strong, slow, forceful turning of the elevator handle:
opts: Moves the tooth posteriorly, expanding bone and tearing the periodontal ligament
Delivers the tooth completely from the socket
mcqs.explain: The elevator step prepares the tooth; the forceps complete the extraction.

mcqs.q: When adapting the forceps, the blades should be placed:
opts: Apical to the cervical line, gripping the root beneath the loosened gingiva
On the crown, coronal to the cervical line
On the occlusal surface of the tooth
mcqs.explain: The lingual blade is usually seated first, then the buccal blade.

mcqs.q: Which blade of the forceps is usually seated first?
mcqs.explain: The buccal blade follows.

mcqs.q: The surgeon grasps the handles of the forceps at the very ends in order to:
opts: Reduce the risk of slipping onto the soft tissue
mcqs.explain: Holding too near the joint loses the lever arm; too far loses control.

mcqs.q: The beaks of the forceps must be held parallel to the long axis of the tooth in order to:
opts: Avoid fracture of the tooth root
Prevent injury to the opposing teeth
Reduce the need for apical pressure
mcqs.explain: Non-parallel beaks concentrate force across the root and fracture it.

mcqs.q: Strong apical pressure during adaptation is applied to:
opts: Expand the crestal bone and displace the centre of rotation as apically as possible
Push the tooth deeper into its socket permanently
Sever the periodontal ligament at the apex
mcqs.explain: The beaks act as wedges to dilate the crestal bone on both buccal and lingual aspects.

mcqs.q: If the centre of rotation is NOT far apically but closer to the occlusal, the result is:
opts: Excessive movement of the tooth apex, causing apex fracture
Failure to expand the socket at all
Fracture of the alveolar crest only
mcqs.explain: This is why strong apical seating comes before any luxating movement.

mcqs.q: For all maxillary and mandibular teeth EXCEPT the mandibular molars, the luxating force is directed:
mcqs.explain: The force goes toward the thinnest and weakest bone, which is buccal everywhere except at the mandibular molars.

mcqs.q: Dilatation of the socket during luxation is accompanied by:
opts: Multiple small fractures on the buccal plate and the inter-radicular septa
A single clean fracture of the lingual plate
Fracture of the tooth apex in every case
mcqs.explain: The bone must have a degree of elasticity to permit expansion, as in younger individuals.

mcqs.q: Removal of the tooth from the socket is performed once:
opts: The alveolar process is sufficiently expanded and the periodontal ligament is completely severed
The forceps have been seated apically
mcqs.explain: This final force is usually directed buccally.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a role of the opposite hand?
opts: Applying the main luxating force to the tooth
Reflecting the cheek, lips and tongue for visualization
Stabilizing the mandible and protecting the TMJ
Supporting the alveolar process and feeling its expansion
mcqs.explain: It also protects other teeth from sudden slipping of the forceps and stabilizes the head.

mcqs.q: The primary movement for extracting the maxillary central incisor is:
opts: Rotation in one direction then the other, because the root is conical and straight
Pure labio-palatal rocking with no rotation
mcqs.explain: Additional labio-palatal movement follows, with final delivery in a labial direction.

mcqs.q: Which forceps is used for the maxillary central incisor?
opts: Upper anterior tooth forceps with wide blades
mcqs.explain: The lateral incisor uses a straight forceps with finer blades.

mcqs.q: The maxillary lateral incisor is more difficult to extract than the central incisor because:
opts: Thicker bone, and a slender root flattened mesio-distally that may curve apically
Its root is conical and relatively short
Its labial bone is unusually thick
mcqs.explain: A straight forceps with finer blades is used and the tooth is delivered labio-incisally.

mcqs.q: For the maxillary lateral incisor, rotation should be:
opts: Avoided, especially if the root is bent
mcqs.explain: The slender, often curved root fractures readily under rotation.

mcqs.q: The maxillary canine is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
opts: It has the thickest labial bone of any maxillary tooth
It is the longest tooth in the mouth
Its oblong root produces the canine eminence
It frequently has an apical curvature
mcqs.explain: The labial bone is thin and sometimes liable to fracture during extraction.

mcqs.q: The maxillary first premolar is known as the “King of fracture” because:
opts: Its buccal and palatal roots are extremely thin and it is the most commonly fractured tooth
Its crown fractures under the forceps
Its palatal bone is extremely thick
mcqs.explain: It is single-rooted in its first two thirds, bifurcating in the apical third to half.

mcqs.q: In the maxillary first premolar, which root is MOST likely to break?
mcqs.explain: The palatal root is the one that is more difficult to retrieve, which is why the palatal movement must be careful.

mcqs.q: Which movement is specifically avoided in the maxillary first premolar?
mcqs.explain: Final delivery is with tractional force in the occluso-buccal direction.

mcqs.q: The maxillary second premolar differs from the first premolar in that it:
opts: Has a single thick root with a blunt end and is less liable to fracture
Has thicker buccal than palatal bone
mcqs.explain: The same upper premolar forceps is used for both.

mcqs.q: The maxillary first molar has:
opts: 3 divergent roots — 2 buccal closer together, the longest palatal diverging palatally
mcqs.explain: It is firmly embedded and further reinforced by the zygomatic bone.

mcqs.q: The particular hazard when extracting the maxillary first molar is:
mcqs.explain: The roots lie in close proximity to the maxillary sinus.

mcqs.q: For the maxillary molars, rotational movements are:
opts: Used only for the third molar
mcqs.explain: Strong bucco-palatal movement, stronger to the buccal, is used instead.

mcqs.q: The maxillary second molar compared with the first molar has roots that are:
opts: Shorter, less divergent, mostly straight, with the buccal roots possibly fused
Always fused into one conical root
mcqs.explain: The same forceps and technique are used, but with greater ease.

mcqs.q: The bayonet third molar forceps is used when:
opts: Accessibility to the upper third molar becomes difficult
mcqs.explain: Teeth with fused roots are usually easily removed; the particular warning is maxillary tuberosity fracture.

mcqs.q: When extracting an upper third molar, one must beware of:
mcqs.explain: The tuberosity lies immediately behind the tooth.

mcqs.q: Rotary movements are contraindicated for the mandibular incisors because:
opts: The roots are very thin and flattened bucco-lingually and are liable to fracture
The lingual bone is too thick
The crowns are too large to grip
mcqs.explain: The supporting alveolar process is also very thin both labially and lingually.

mcqs.q: Which forceps is used for the mandibular canine?
mcqs.explain: The same technique as for the incisors is used, but greater force is required.

mcqs.q: Forceps with slightly curving blades are used for the mandibular premolars in order to:
opts: Grip the neck while avoiding pressure on the large crown
mcqs.explain: The forceps are then forced apically as far as possible.

mcqs.q: For the mandibular SECOND premolar, the first movement is:
mcqs.explain: It is one of only two teeth in which rotation is indicated, because of its conical root.

mcqs.q: Comparing the mandibular molars:
opts: The roots of the first molar are more widely divergent than those of the second molar
The roots of the second molar are more widely divergent
The first molar has three roots
mcqs.explain: Both have 2 heavy and strong roots.

mcqs.q: In the mandibular third molar, the cortical plate that is thinner is the:
mcqs.explain: This reverses the usual mandibular pattern and is why elevators are often needed.

mcqs.q: When the mandibular third molar is inaccessible to forceps, the elevator blade is inserted:
opts: Mesiobuccally, using the interdental septum as fulcrum
Distolingually, using the ramus as fulcrum
Directly apically along the long axis
mcqs.explain: After luxation of the tooth, the forceps should complete the extraction.

mcqs.q: Sharp bony edges and projecting septae are trimmed after extraction in order to:
opts: Avoid pain, promote healing and allow a proper alveolar ridge for dentures
Prevent entry of saliva into the socket
mcqs.explain: Removing tooth fragments, broken filling material and calculus prevents postoperative infection.

mcqs.q: Squeezing the socket with the thumb and index fingers after extraction achieves all the following EXCEPT:
opts: Prevention of postoperative pain and infection by keeping out saliva with food debris and bacteria
Promotion of rapid healing and a more ideal ridge shape
mcqs.explain: The granuloma is removed by curettage, and only if a periapical lesion is present.

mcqs.q: The gauze pressure pack must NOT fall inside the socket because it would:
opts: Interfere with organization of the blood clot
Cause fracture of the alveolar plates
Prevent the patient from closing the teeth
mcqs.explain: The patient is asked to bite on the pack placed over the wound.

mcqs.q: Before dismissing the patient, the operator must:
mcqs.explain: The lip and face should also be cleaned of any traces of blood.

mcqs.q: If a periapical granuloma is not removed during extraction:
opts: The alveolar ridge will resorb completely
mcqs.explain: The socket should be debrided only if necessary — a periapical lesion is curetted to remove the granuloma or cyst.

mcqs.q: When a tooth is removed because of periodontal disease, the socket may contain:
opts: Excess granulation tissue, which should be removed
Retained root fragments in every case
mcqs.explain: This is one of the three stated indications for debriding the socket.

mcqs.q: The moistened gauze placed over the socket should be positioned so that:
opts: When the patient closes the teeth together, it fits the space previously occupied by the crown
It is pushed firmly into the depth of the socket
It lies on the buccal mucosa only
mcqs.explain: The pressure of biting is then transmitted to the socket, resulting in homeostasis.

mcqs.q: For how long should the patient keep biting pressure on the gauze sponges?
mcqs.explain: No mouthwash is allowed for 12 hours.

mcqs.q: Mouthwash should be avoided for how long after extraction?
mcqs.explain: A warm antiseptic or saline mouthwash begins the day after, at 12–24 hours.

mcqs.q: Cold applications on the extraction site are advised:
opts: Intermittently, about 20 min per hour, for the rest of the day of surgery only
Only if swelling has already appeared
mcqs.explain: They relieve pain and minimize post-operative facial swelling.

mcqs.q: Warm antiseptic or saline mouthwash should be started:
opts: The day after extraction, 12–24 hours postoperatively, 3–5 times daily for a few days
mcqs.explain: Cold is for the day of surgery; warm rinses start the following day.

mcqs.q: Which post-operative instruction protects the blood clot from being dislodged by suction and heat?
opts: See the dentist in case of complications
mcqs.explain: The recommended diet is cold fluids or soft food to avoid irritating the wound.

saqs.q: List the methods of extraction and describe the five major motions that the forceps can apply.
saqs.a: METHODS — simple (closed, forceps, intra-alveolar) and surgical (open, trans-alveolar). FIVE MOTIONS — apical pressure, buccal force, lingual/palatal pressure, rotational pressure, tractional force.

head: Motion
Effect
rows: the beaks are inserted into the periodontal ligament space and act as a wedge, expanding the alveolar bone and displacing the tooth occlusally
expands the buccal alveolar plate, particularly at the crest of the ridge, with lingual apical pressure
causes internal expansion of the socket. Best for conical single roots; slender or multi-rooted teeth fracture under it, so rotation is limited to the upper central incisor and lower second premolar
delivers the tooth once adequate bony expansion is achieved — limited to the final portion of the extraction, and gentle

saqs.q: Explain how the thickness of the alveolar bone determines the direction of force in each jaw.
saqs.a: The major force goes toward the THINNEST, weakest bone. MAXILLA — buccal bone thinner than palatal, so strong buccal and less vigorous palatal. MANDIBLE — buccal bone thinner from midline to premolars, so incisors, canines and premolars take strong buccal force; mandibular MOLARS have stronger buccal bone and need stronger LINGUAL pressure.

ans.text: Most teeth are removed by a combination of buccal and lingual forces, with the major portion directed toward the thinnest and therefore weakest bone.

head: Region
Bone
Main force
rows: buccal bone thinner than palatal cortical bone
buccal bone thinner from the midline posteriorly to the premolars

saqs.q: Describe the five general steps of forceps extraction.
saqs.a: 1 Loosen the soft tissue attachment with the No. 9 Molt. 2 Luxate with a straight elevator if indicated. 3 Adapt the forceps apical to the cervical line, lingual blade first, gripping the handle ends. 4 Luxate with the forceps toward the thinnest bone, slow steady force. 5 Remove the tooth once the process is expanded and the PDL severed, usually buccally.

steps: Loosen the soft tissue attachment — with the sharp end of a periosteal elevator (No. 9 Molt), so the forceps can seat more apically; slight reflection widens the gingival sulcus for the beak tips

Luxate with a dental elevator, if indicated — a straight elevator perpendicular or parallel to the tooth in the interdental space, with strong slow forceful turning, expanding bone and tearing the PDL

Adapt the forceps — blades apical to the cervical line, tips grasping root under the loosened gingiva, lingual blade first, then buccal; grasp the handles at the very ends for maximum mechanical advantage

Luxate with the forceps — force toward the thinnest, weakest bone (labial/buccal for all except mandibular molars); slow steady force, gradually increasing, then the opposite direction. Dilatation is accompanied by small fractures of the buccal plate and inter-radicular septa
Remove the tooth — once the alveolar process is sufficiently expanded and the PDL completely severed, force usually directed buccally

saqs.q: Describe the correct grip and adaptation of the forceps, and explain the significance of the centre of rotation.
saqs.a: Adapt the blades apical to the cervical line, lingual blade first, grasping the handles at the very ends — not near or far from the joint. Keep the beaks PARALLEL to the long axis to avoid root fracture. Strong apical pressure displaces the CENTRE OF ROTATION as apically as possible; if it stays near the occlusal, the apex moves excessively and fractures.

list: Blades adapted to the tooth apical to the cervical line, tips grasping the root under the loosened gingiva — lingual blade first, then buccal
Grasp the handles at the very ends for maximum mechanical advantage and control — a grip too near or too far from the joint is wrong
Hold the beaks PARALLEL to the long axis of the tooth, to avoid fracturing the root

ans.text: The beaks act as wedges dilating the crestal bone buccally and lingually, and strong apical pressure displaces the CENTRE OF ROTATION as apically as possible. If the centre of rotation is not far apically, it sits closer to the occlusal — causing excessive movement of the tooth apex and apex fracture.

saqs.q: List the roles of the opposite hand during extraction.
saqs.a: Reflect the soft tissue of cheek, lips and tongue for visualization · protect other teeth from sudden slipping of the forceps · stabilize the patient's head · stabilize the mandible, protecting the TMJ from undue force · support the alveolar process and feel its expansion.

list: Reflect the soft tissue of the cheek, lips and tongue for adequate visualization
Protect other teeth from sudden slipping of the forceps
Stabilize the patient's head
Stabilize the mandible, protecting the TMJ from undue forces
Support the alveolar process, giving tactile information about its expansion

saqs.q: Describe the technique for extracting the maxillary anterior teeth — central incisor, lateral incisor and canine.
saqs.a: CENTRAL INCISOR — wide-blade forceps; primary ROTATION (conical straight root), then labio-palatal, delivered labially. LATERAL INCISOR — harder, thicker bone, slender root flattened mesiodistally, often curved apically; finer blades, labio-incisal with slight traction, AVOID rotation. CANINE — the longest tooth, oblong root (canine eminence), thin labial bone liable to fracture; wide blades, labial then palatal, slight rotation may help.

head: Tooth
Anatomy
Technique
rows: conical, straight root; buccal bone thinner
upper anterior forceps with wide blades; primary ROTATION one way then the other, then labio-palatal movement, delivered labially
embedded in thicker bone; root slender, flattened mesially and distally, often tapering to a fine point, apex may be curved
straight forceps with finer blades; delivered labio-incisally with a small amount of traction — avoid rotation, especially if the root is bent
the longest tooth; root oblong in cross section, producing the canine eminence, frequently with apical curvature; thin labial bone, liable to fracture
straight forceps with wide blades; initial movement labial with return pressure palatally; a small amount of rotation may help expand the socket

saqs.q: Compare the extraction of the maxillary first and second premolars.
saqs.a: FIRST PREMOLAR — single-rooted for two thirds then bifurcates bucco-lingually in the apical third; thin roots, the most commonly fractured tooth (the 'King of fracture'). Initial buccal then careful palatal; buccal root most likely to break; NO rotation; delivered occluso-buccally. SECOND PREMOLAR — single thick blunt root, less liable to fracture; primary buccal back to palate, then bucco-occlusal traction. Same forceps for both.

head: FIRST premolar
SECOND premolar
rows: single-rooted in its first two thirds, bifurcating buccolingually in the apical third to half; roots extremely thin
a single thick root with a blunt end
the most commonly fractured tooth — the 'King of fracture'
buccal bone relatively thin compared with palatal
as with all maxillary teeth, buccal bone is thinner

initial buccal, then careful palatal to avoid fracturing the palatal root (harder to retrieve); the buccal root is most likely to break; avoid any rotation; final delivery by traction occluso-buccally
primary buccal movement back to the palate, then a final bucco-occlusal traction force

saqs.q: Describe the extraction of the maxillary molars.
saqs.a: FIRST MOLAR — three divergent roots (two buccal closer, the strongest longest palatal diverging palatally), firmly embedded and reinforced by the zygoma; beware the sinus. Strong bucco-palatal, stronger buccally; NO rotation. SECOND MOLAR — same but shorter, less divergent, mostly straight roots that may be fused; same technique, easier. THIRD MOLAR — variable, often conical fused roots; molar forceps, or Bayonet third-molar forceps if access is difficult; beware tuberosity fracture.

head: Tooth
Anatomy and technique
rows: three divergent roots — two buccal closer together, and the strongest, longest palatal root diverging palatally. Firmly embedded, reinforced by the zygomatic bone; beware proximity to the maxillary sinus (perforation is liable). Strong bucco-palatal movement, stronger to the buccal — avoiding fracture of the more difficult palatal root, and because buccal cortical bone is thinner. Rotation is contraindicated
like the first, but roots are shorter and less divergent, mostly straight, and the buccal roots may be fused. Same forceps and technique — but with greater ease

great variation in root number and form; frequently conical roots that may be fused, sometimes resembling the first and second molars. The same molar forceps; where access is difficult, the Bayonet third-molar forceps. Fused roots are usually easy — but beware maxillary tuberosity fracture

saqs.q: Describe the extraction of the mandibular teeth.
saqs.a: INCISORS — roots flattened buccolingually, very thin; NO rotation; thin labial and lingual plates; lower anterior forceps. CANINE — one laterally flattened root, stronger and longer; lower premolar forceps, same technique, more force. PREMOLARS — large crowns, slightly curved blades to grip the neck; buccal then lingual; second premolar starts with rotation, delivered occluso-buccally. MOLARS — two heavy roots, first more divergent; beaks parallel to the long axis, strong buccolingual, delivered bucco-occlusally. THIRD MOLAR — lingual plate thinner; often needs an elevator mesiobuccally on the interdental septum, then forceps.

head: Tooth
Anatomy and technique
rows: roots flattened bucco-lingually; central shorter, lateral may be curved. Roots very thin and liable to fracture, so rotary movements are contraindicated; the supporting process is very thin both labially and lingually. Lower anterior forceps
one root flattened laterally, stronger and longer than the incisors. Lower premolar forceps and the same technique, but greater force required

large crowns, so forceps with slightly curving blades grip the neck without pressing the crown. Force apically as far as possible; movements buccal returning to lingual. For the second premolar, the first movement is rotation, then delivery occluso-buccally

two heavy, strong roots, the first molar's more widely divergent. Beaks pushed apically as far as possible, long axis parallel to the tooth; strong buccolingual motion expands the socket, delivery bucco-occlusally

the lingual cortical plate is thinner than the buccal. Often inaccessible to forceps, so elevators are indicated — blade inserted mesiobuccally using the interdental septum as fulcrum; after luxation the forceps completes the extraction

saqs.q: List the post-extraction procedures performed immediately after the tooth is removed.
saqs.a: Remove fragments, filling pieces and calculus from the socket · trim and smooth sharp bony edges · squeeze the socket with thumb and index finger to reposition the plates · apply a gauze pressure pack for the patient to bite on (it must not fall into the socket) · clean the lip and face · do not dismiss the patient until bleeding is controlled.

steps: Remove any tooth fragment, broken filling material or calculus that might fall into the socket — preventing postoperative infection
Trim and smooth sharp bony edges and projecting bony septae — avoiding pain, promoting healing, and allowing a proper alveolar ridge for dentures
Squeeze the socket with thumb and index finger, adapting the dilated plates and their soft tissue back to position
Apply a pressure pack of gauze over the wound and ask the patient to bite — the pack must not fall inside the socket, where it would interfere with organization of the clot
Clean the lip and face of any traces of blood
Do not dismiss the patient before examining for controlled bleeding

list: Control of bleeding
Prevention of postoperative pain and infection — narrowing the opening keeps out saliva loaded with debris and bacteria
Promotion of rapid healing
A more ideal alveolar ridge shape

ans.text: A moistened gauze is positioned so that when the patient closes, it fits the space the crown occupied — transmitting biting pressure to the socket and producing homeostasis.

saqs.q: When should the socket be debrided, and why?
saqs.a: Only if necessary. With a PERIAPICAL LESION, curette the periapical region to remove the granuloma or cyst — otherwise a residual cyst forms. If the tooth was removed for PERIODONTAL DISEASE, excess granulation tissue may have accumulated and should be removed.

ans.text: The socket should be debrided only if necessary.

head: Situation
Why
rows: curette the periapical region to remove the granuloma or cyst — a residual cyst will form if it is left
excess granulation tissue may have accumulated and should be removed

saqs.q: List the post-operative instructions given to the patient.
saqs.a: Bite on the gauze for one hour · no mouthwash for 12 hours · avoid hot food and drink that day · take a suitable analgesic · apply cold intermittently ~20 min per hour on the day of surgery only · cold fluids or soft food · warm antiseptic or saline mouthwash from 12–24 hours after, 3–5 times daily for a few days · avoid smoking · return if complications occur.

list: Keep biting pressure on the gauze for one hour
No mouthwash for 12 hours
Avoid hot food and drink for the rest of the day
Take a suitable analgesic
Apply cold intermittently, about 20 minutes per hour, for the day of surgery only — relieving pain and minimising facial swelling
Diet — cold fluids or soft food, to avoid irritating the wound
Warm antiseptic or saline mouthwash from 12–24 hours after, 3–5 times daily, continued for a few days
Avoid smoking
See your dentist again in case of complications
